title: The peace chant — purnam adah, purnam idam — from fullness, fullness (5.1)
hook: light a candle from a candle and the first flame loses nothing: the great line we leave the Brihadaranyaka on, chanted all over the world
tomorrow: the teacher's charge to the student: "speak the truth, practice dharma"

segments.voice: Yesterday: neti, neti, not this, not this, and Yajnavalkya finally went away. Your line was not this, not this.

Light a candle, and use it to light a second one. Look at the first flame: it hasn't gotten any smaller. Light ten more from it, a hundred, and it's still exactly as bright. Something was given away completely, and nothing was lost. At a Hindu gathering, a yoga class, or the start of an Upanishad recital, you may have heard a short Sanskrit chant that ends om shanti, shanti, shanti. It comes from the opening of the Brihadaranyaka's fifth book, and it's where this path leaves the book.
screen: `A CANDLE LIGHTS A CANDLE.` → `THE FIRST FLAME LOSES NOTHING.` → `A CHANT HEARD AT THE START OF STUDY.`

segments.voice: Here it is. Purnam adah purnam idam purnat purnam udacyate, purnasya purnam adaya purnam evavashishyate. That is full. This is full. From the full, the full comes forth. Take the full from the full, and the full alone remains. Purna means full, whole, complete, lacking nothing. That is the far side, Brahman beyond everything you can point to. This is the near side, the world right here, the one you're sitting in. And the chant refuses to make either one the lesser half. The world doesn't come out of Brahman like a slice out of a cake, leaving a hole. It comes out like a flame from a flame. People who love mathematics sometimes hear infinity in it: take infinity from infinity, and infinity is left. The tradition attaches it as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad, too, and it's chanted at the start of study, worship and gatherings. And it's a fitting place to finish the Brihadaranyaka. Look back down this great forest of a book. The horse that was the whole cosmos. Death's hunger making a world. The breath the demons couldn't pierce. I am, then fear, then longing. The self split into two halves. Maitreyi setting aside the earth. Salt with no inside or outside. Honey for each other. A thousand cows, challenger after challenger, a head that fell. The light of the self, the dreamer, deep sleep, the caterpillar, desire. Not this, not this. And at the end, not emptiness. Fullness. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad, the Taittiriya, and a teacher's speech to his graduating students.
screen: `THAT IS FULL. THIS IS FULL.` · `A FLAME FROM A FLAME, NOT A SLICE.` · `THE PEACE CHANT OF STUDY AND WORSHIP.` · `THE WHOLE FOREST OF A BOOK.` · then, large: `FULL FROM FULL.`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, let the word come: full; on the out-breath: full. See whether the breath you just gave away left you lacking anything, with the next one already arriving. If you like, say the chant silently, or just its first line, purnam adah, purnam idam, and let the words and the breath move together until the words fall away.
Purna, full, whole, complete. In the peace chant, what that is, what this is, and what remains when the full is taken from the full.
Your line: full from full. The world isn't a slice taken out of Brahman. Rest well.

howItsDone: The purnam adah chant is recited as the shanti mantra of the Isha Upanishad and of the Shukla Yajurveda tradition, at the start and end of study, at pujas and at many gatherings, followed by om shanti, shanti, shanti.

original.note: Sanskrit pūrṇam: full, whole, complete. pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam, that is full, this is full.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty chant to start a yoga class.
what it means: that and this, the beyond and the world, are both whole, and giving one from the other loses nothing.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 5.1.1, also the śānti-pāṭha of the Isha Upanishad; Shankara reads 'that' as the unmanifest and 'this' as the manifest.

chat.says: What does the 'purnam adah, purnam idam' chant actually mean?
options: That is full, this is full; take the full from the full, and the full remains.
Give everything away, and in the end you'll be left with nothing at all.
It's a prayer asking for a full harvest and full granaries this year.
chat.meaning: Purna means full. That, Brahman, is full; this, the world, is full; the world comes from Brahman like a flame from a flame.

om shanti.meaning: peace; often said three times to close a prayer

Brahman.meaning: the great reality; here, that, the far side

Isha Upanishad.meaning: a short Upanishad that opens with this same peace chant

Taittiriya.meaning: the Upanishad this path reads next

Maitreyi.meaning: Yajnavalkya's wife, who set aside the earth's wealth
